title: Pomeroy WWII Journals: An OCR Transcription Pipeline
text:
Preface
This document is a transcription of the WWII journals of Dr.Richard Pomeroy. It contains three typewritten volumes (364 pages), two from military deployment 1943-1945 and one from a family trip to Europe in 1966.
The source scans are available as a download from Google Drive here:

Download Dr. Richard Pomeroy’s WWII (1943-1945) and Travel Journals (1966)

This book documents the transcription code pipeline and publishes the resulting documents. Downloads of the transcription (DOCX, searchable PDF, and per-page CSV) are linked in the Assembly chapter.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.1 Goals
The aim is a readable, searchable transcription of Dr. Richard Pomeroy’s typewritten journals, produced by a pipeline that anyone can rerun and inspect. Three principles guide the work:

title: 1  Overview
text:
Automate what can be automated. Optical character recognition (OCR) handles the bulk of the text. People are asked to type or check only the pages the software handles poorly.
Stay near-verbatim. The text is not modernised or silently corrected. Where the OCR is unsure of a word, the word is flagged. Every human fix is recorded in a single file, data/corrections.csv, so each change can be traced.
Keep the record reproducible. One command, targets::tar_make(), rebuilds everything from the scans, and every script is shown in full in this book. Package versions are pinned and the settings that differ between volumes live in one file. See Setup for the steps. Rendering the book never reruns OCR.

The WWII volume numbering is not yet confirmed, so the book refers to the files by name.
The preface quotes 364 pages, while the PDFs contain 378 (102 + 188 + 88). The difference has not been reconciled. Front matter in the 1966 journal and duplicated pages in the scans are likely contributors.

title: 1  Overview
text:
1.4 Rights and ethics
The journals are family papers. The owner has agreed to their public release, including the names they contain. The scans themselves are not stored in this repository; they are shared through the download link in the preface.

title: 2  Setup and Reproducing the Work
text:
2.1 Rebuilding from scratch
This chapter says what is needed to rebuild the transcription from the scanned PDFs, and shows the file that runs every step in order. Every script the project uses is shown in full in the chapter for its step. The only things not generated by code are the three scans, the settings file data/volume_config.csv (described below) and the human corrections in data/corrections.csv.
With the three PDFs saved as data/raw_pdf/vol1.pdf, vol2.pdf and vol3.pdf:
Step 3 is the single entry point. It profiles every page, downloads any missing Tesseract language data, crops and OCRs all 378 pages, builds the triage tables, runs the settings experiments and applies the corrections. It takes roughly 30 minutes on a six-core machine (about 4 minutes for the inventory, 20 for OCR, the rest for tiering and experiments). Steps whose inputs have not changed are skipped on a rerun, and OCR results are cached page by page, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped.
Show code
# The whole pipeline, from the scanned PDFs to the final tables. Run with
#   targets::tar_make()
# Steps whose inputs have not changed are skipped; OCR results are also cached
# page by page in data/interim/ocr/, so an interrupted run resumes.
library(targets)
tar_source("R")
tar_option_set(packages = c("tidyverse", "pdftools", "magick", "tesseract"))

list(
  # Inputs: per-volume settings and the scans
  tar_target(config_file, "data/volume_config.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(config, read_csv(config_file, show_col_types = FALSE)),
  tar_target(pdf_files, file.path("data/raw_pdf", config$file), format = "file"),

  # Step 1: profile every page (blank, duplicate and layout checks)
  tar_target(inventory_file, run_inventory(config, pdf_files), format = "file"),

  # Step 2: crop, render and OCR every page
  tar_target(languages, ensure_languages(config)),
  tar_target(ocr_files, run_ocr(config, pdf_files, languages), format = "file"),

  # Step 3: tiers, draft text, review images, manual queue
  tar_target(output_files, build_outputs(config, ocr_files), format = "file"),

  # Step 4: settings experiments reported in the book
  tar_target(experiment_files, run_experiments(ocr_files), format = "file"),

  # Step 5: final text = OCR draft with the human corrections applied
  tar_target(corrections_file, "data/corrections.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(final, {
    output_files
    apply_corrections(corr_path = corrections_file)
  })
)

title: 3  Page Extraction
text:
3.1 Inventory
Extraction turns each PDF page into a 300 DPI PNG named vol1_p001.png, ready for OCR. It has two parts: a quick inventory of every page, and, for the spread scans, cropping to the page that holds text.
Before extracting anything, each page is rendered at low resolution and profiled for ink amount, size and similarity to other pages. This finds blank pages, near-duplicate pages and the layout of each volume.
One measurement choice mattered. Typewriter strokes are thin and wash out at low resolution, so an absolute darkness cutoff misses real text. “Ink” is therefore measured relative to each page’s own median brightness.
Show code
# Inventory step: profile every page at low DPI to find blank pages, duplicate
# pages (24x24 block-mean signature) and front matter. Run per volume.
# Typewriter strokes are thin and wash out at 30 DPI, so "ink" is measured
# relative to each page's own median luminance, not an absolute threshold.
library(pdftools)
library(tidyverse)

block_mean <- function(m, n = 24) {
  ri <- cut(seq_len(nrow(m)), n, labels = FALSE)
  ci <- cut(seq_len(ncol(m)), n, labels = FALSE)
  as.vector(tapply(m, list(factor(ri, 1:n)[row(m)], factor(ci, 1:n)[col(m)]), mean))
}

profile_page <- function(pdf, page, dpi = 40) {
  a <- pdf_render_page(pdf, page = page, dpi = dpi, numeric = TRUE)
  g <- (a[, , 1] + a[, , 2] + a[, , 3]) / 3
  h <- nrow(g); w <- ncol(g)
  cut_at <- median(g) - 0.12
  ink <- function(m) mean(m < cut_at)
  trim <- function(m) m[round(h * .06):round(h * .94), ]
  tibble(
    width_px = w, height_px = h, mean_lum = mean(g), sd_lum = sd(g),
    ink = ink(trim(g[, round(w * .06):round(w * .94)])),
    ink_left = ink(trim(g[, round(w * .06):round(w * .5)])),
    ink_right = ink(trim(g[, round(w * .5):round(w * .94)])),
    sig = list(block_mean(g))
  )
}

profile_volume <- function(file, dpi = 40) {
  pdf <- file.path("data/raw_pdf", file)
  vol <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(file)
  tibble(file = file, page_id = sprintf("%s_p%03d", vol, seq_len(pdf_info(pdf)$pages))) |>
    mutate(page = row_number(), prof = map(page, \(p) profile_page(pdf, p, dpi))) |>
    unnest(prof)
}

flag_pages <- function(inv, blank_ink = 0.003, dup_dist = 0.15) {
  sigm <- do.call(rbind, inv$sig)
  d <- as.matrix(dist(sigm)); diag(d) <- Inf
  nn <- apply(d, 1, which.min)
  inv |>
    mutate(
      orientation = if_else(width_px > height_px, "landscape", "portrait"),
      is_blank = ink < blank_ink,
      nearest_page = nn,
      nearest_dist = d[cbind(seq_along(nn), nn)],
      possible_dup = nearest_dist < dup_dist
    ) |>
    select(-sig)
}

# Inventory every PDF listed in the config and write one table. Duplicate
# detection runs over all pages together, so a repeat across files (such as
# vol1 p102 and vol3 p1) is found too.
run_inventory <- function(config, pdf_files = NULL, out = "data/interim/page_inventory.csv", dpi = 40) {
  inv <- map(config$file, profile_volume, dpi = dpi) |> list_rbind() |> flag_pages()
  inv <- inv |>
    mutate(nearest_id = page_id[nearest_page]) |>
    select(-nearest_page)
  dir.create(dirname(out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  write_csv(inv, out)
  out
}

title: 3  Page Extraction
text:
vol2.pdf has no blank or duplicate pages. Its first six pages are front matter (a three-page table of contents, an itinerary and a mail schedule); entries begin on page 7, giving 182 entry pages. A few sparse pages are short text, not blanks.
vol1.pdf and vol3.pdf carry text on the right half of every spread. In vol1.pdf, pages 1 and 44 to 46 are portrait pages.
Some pages look like duplicates: vol1 pages 77 and 78, and 96 and 97 (near-identical). vol1 page 102 also appears to repeat vol3 page 1, but the match is weaker: each is the other’s nearest page, at a distance of 0.165, just outside the 0.15 cutoff. It is recorded in the config. None has been removed yet.

title: 3  Page Extraction
text:
3.2 Cropping spreads
A spread contains a text page, a mostly blank facing page and a dark binding shadow. Splitting every spread down the middle would leave shadow in the OCR input, so the crop is detected per page:

Render the spread at 100 DPI and find the spine, the darkest lines near the centre, plus any graded shadow touching it.
Trim scan borders on the outer edge and at the top and bottom.
Apply the detected box to a 300 DPI render of the same page.



Show code
# Crop a scanned spread to its text page and trim the binding shadow and scan
# borders. Geometry is detected on a cheap low-DPI render, then applied to the
# full-resolution render. Only the right-hand page holds text in vol1/vol3
# (see data/volume_config.csv), so side = "right" is the default.
library(pdftools)
library(magick)
library(tidyverse)

gray_matrix <- function(img) {
  a <- image_data(image_convert(img, colorspace = "gray"), channels = "gray")
  # rows = x (columns of the picture), cols = y
  matrix(as.integer(a[1, , ]), nrow = dim(a)[2]) / 255
}

# last/first run helpers: extend a boundary while the profile stays dark
extend_while_dark <- function(is_dark, start, dir, max_steps) {
  pos <- start
  for (i in seq_len(max_steps)) {
    nxt <- pos + dir
    if (nxt < 1 || nxt > length(is_dark) || !is_dark[nxt]) break
    pos <- nxt
  }
  pos
}

# Returns fractional box (x0, x1, y0, y1) of the text page, in 0-1 of the spread
detect_text_box <- function(m, side = "right", dark_drop = 0.1, pad = 0.01) {
  w <- nrow(m); h <- ncol(m)
  colmed <- apply(m, 1, median)
  paper <- quantile(colmed[round(w * .55):round(w * .9)], .9)
  dark <- colmed < paper - dark_drop

  # Spine: darkest lines near the centre, then any graded shadow touching them
  centre <- round(w * .4):round(w * .6)
  spine <- centre[dark[centre]]
  spine_end <- if (length(spine)) max(spine) else round(w * .5)
  colmean <- colMeans(t(m))
  graded <- colmean < mean(colmean[round(w * .55):round(w * .9)]) - 0.04
  spine_end <- extend_while_dark(graded, spine_end, +1, round(w * .06))
  x0 <- spine_end + round(w * pad)

  # Outer scan border on the far edge
  edge <- round(w * .93):w
  edge_dark <- edge[dark[edge]]
  x1 <- if (length(edge_dark)) min(edge_dark) - round(w * pad) else w

  # Top/bottom borders, measured over the text page only
  rowmed <- apply(m[x0:x1, , drop = FALSE], 2, median)
  rdark <- rowmed < median(rowmed) - dark_drop
  top <- which(rdark[seq_len(round(h * .06))])
  bot <- which(rdark) |> keep(\(y) y > h * .94)
  y0 <- if (length(top)) max(top) + round(h * pad) else 1
  y1 <- if (length(bot)) min(bot) - round(h * pad) else h

  if (side == "left") stop("left-side text is not used in these volumes")
  c(x0 = x0 / w, x1 = x1 / w, y0 = y0 / h, y1 = y1 / h)
}

# page: 1-based PDF page. Returns a magick image at out_dpi.
crop_text_half <- function(pdf, page, out_dpi = 300, detect_dpi = 100, side = "right") {
  render <- function(dpi) {
    f <- file.path("data/interim", sprintf("render_%s_%03d_%d.png",
                                           tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(pdf)), page, dpi))
    on.exit(unlink(f))
    pdf_convert(pdf, pages = page, dpi = dpi, format = "png", filenames = f, verbose = FALSE)
    image_read(f)
  }
  box <- detect_text_box(gray_matrix(render(detect_dpi)), side = side)
  hi <- render(out_dpi)
  info <- image_info(hi)
  geom <- geometry_area(
    width = round((box[["x1"]] - box[["x0"]]) * info$width),
    height = round((box[["y1"]] - box[["y0"]]) * info$height),
    x_off = round(box[["x0"]] * info$width),
    y_off = round(box[["y0"]] * info$height)
  )
  # repage drops the virtual canvas offset left by the crop
  image_crop(hi, geom, repage = FALSE)
}


The method worked on nine test pages. It leaves some shadow at the left edge of vol3 page 88 and a small dark corner on vol3 page 60.

title: 3  Page Extraction
4  Quality Triage
text:
4.1 Flagging words
Not every page needs the same attention. After OCR, each page is scored and placed in one of three tiers, so effort goes where it is needed.
Tesseract reports a confidence for every word. A word is flagged for review if either of these holds:
Names and places are not in the dictionary, so they are flagged too. That adds noise but is harmless: a flag only asks a person to look. The opposite error is not caught. A real word that OCR misreads as a different real word, with high confidence, is not flagged.

text:

it is not in the spelling package’s English dictionary.

title: 4  Quality Triage
text:
4.2 Tiers
A page’s tier depends on the share of its words that are flagged.








Tier
Rule
Treatment




A, manual
25% or more of words flagged, fewer than 40 words, or forced
Type from the scan


B, proofread
10% to 25% flagged
Fix flagged words


C, spot check
Under 10% flagged
Spot check only



“Forced” pages are listed in the force_manual_pages column of data/volume_config.csv: the 1966 front matter (pages 1 to 6) and the two-column newsletter pages in vol3 (87 and 88), where tesseract’s output is known to be unreliable regardless of its confidence.

title: 4  Quality Triage
text:
4.3 Limits
The cutoffs above have not been tuned. Tuning needs hand-typed reference pages, which do not exist yet (see Local OCR). Treat the tiers as a sensible first sort, not a measured quality grade. A file of manual overrides, data/triage_overrides.csv, is planned so a person can move a page between tiers; it has not been created.

title: 4  Quality Triage
5  Local OCR
5  Local OCR
text:
5.2 Settings that were tried
Two small experiments ran on the prepared page images, with the code below. Both are rerun by the pipeline and their results are saved in data/interim/experiments/, so the numbers in this chapter are regenerated, not typed in.


Show code
# Tuning experiments behind the choices described in the "Local OCR" chapter.
# Both run on the prepared page images (data/pages/), so run the OCR step
# first. Results are written to data/interim/experiments/ and read by the book.
library(tidyverse)
library(magick)
library(tesseract)

# Ten pages that cover every layout: portrait singles, a TOC, spreads, a
# faded-ribbon page and a two-column page
sample_ids <- c("vol1_p001", "vol1_p044", "vol1_p070", "vol2_p001", "vol2_p040",
                "vol2_p120", "vol3_p002", "vol3_p020", "vol3_p066", "vol3_p087")

ocr_stats <- function(img, psm = 3) {
  raw <- image_write(image_convert(img, colorspace = "gray"), format = "png")
  d <- ocr_data(raw, engine = tesseract("eng", options = list(tessedit_pageseg_mode = as.character(psm))))
  tibble(words = nrow(d), mean_conf = mean(d$confidence), pct_below_80 = mean(d$confidence < 80) * 100)
}

# Page-segmentation modes 3 (automatic), 4 (single column), 6 (single block)
compare_psm <- function(ids = sample_ids, psms = c(3, 4, 6)) {
  expand_grid(page_id = ids, psm = psms) |>
    mutate(stats = map2(page_id, psm, \(id, m) ocr_stats(image_read(file.path("data/pages", paste0(id, ".png"))), m))) |>
    unnest(stats)
}

# Preprocessing variants on one page from each of three kinds of page
preprocess_variants <- list(
  baseline = identity,
  threshold = \(img) img |> image_convert(colorspace = "gray") |>
    image_threshold("white", "55%") |> image_threshold("black", "55%"),
  contrast = \(img) image_contrast(img, sharpen = 1)
)

compare_preprocessing <- function(ids = c("vol1_p010", "vol2_p040", "vol3_p020")) {
  expand_grid(page_id = ids, variant = names(preprocess_variants)) |>
    mutate(stats = map2(page_id, variant, \(id, v) {
      img <- image_read(file.path("data/pages", paste0(id, ".png")))
      ocr_stats(preprocess_variants[[v]](img))
    })) |>
    unnest(stats)
}

run_experiments <- function(ocr_files = NULL, dir = "data/interim/experiments") {
  dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  paths <- c(psm = file.path(dir, "psm_comparison.csv"),
             preprocessing = file.path(dir, "preprocessing_comparison.csv"))
  write_csv(compare_psm(), paths[["psm"]])
  write_csv(compare_preprocessing(), paths[["preprocessing"]])
  unname(paths)
}

On ordinary pages the three modes are within a point or two of each other. The difference appears on the two-column page (vol3_p087): psm 6 reads across both columns as one block and scores about ten points lower with more words, which is the signature of merged columns. psm 3 was used for the full pass as a reasonable default. Mean confidence is only a proxy for accuracy, so this is not a proven best.

title: 5  Local OCR
text:
5.3 What is still unknown
The choice of mode, preprocessing and languages should be made by comparing OCR output with hand-typed text and computing the character error rate. No such reference pages exist yet. When they do, the comparison should cover each layout: clean portrait, spread, faded ribbon, two-column and front matter.

title: 5  Local OCR
text:
5.4 Languages
The first pass used English only. The 1966 journal has German, French and Dutch names, which English-only OCR tends to garble. The config asks for eng+deu+fra for volume 2, and the pipeline installs the missing models and redoes the pages whose cached result used different languages. Rerun before reviewing volume 2: saved corrections replace the OCR text for their page, so a later rerun would not improve pages already corrected.

title: 6  Vision-Model Fallback
text:
6.1 Intended design
Tesseract struggles with some pages: front matter with dotted leaders, dark two-column newsletter pages, and the worn-ribbon section of volume 1. A vision language model, which reads the image directly, may do better on those. The plan is to try it only on the tier A pages, not the whole set.

title: 6  Vision-Model Fallback
text:
Scope. Tier A pages, starting with the 1966 front matter (table of contents, itinerary, mail schedule), the two vol3 newsletter pages and the faded vol1 pages.
Interface. The ellmer package, so the provider can be swapped.
Output. Plain text for ordinary pages and Markdown tables for the schedules, saved next to the tesseract result with the engine recorded.
Caching. Every response is stored per page, so reruns never pay twice.
Review. Model output goes through the same proofreading app. A model transcription is a better starting draft, not a final text.

title: 6  Vision-Model Fallback
text:
6.2 Comparison before committing
Models differ in accuracy and cost. Before using one at scale, two or three providers should transcribe the same ten hand-typed pages. The comparison reports character error rate and cost per page, and the cheaper model wins unless it is clearly less accurate. The model identifiers will be chosen at that point, because the available versions change quickly.

title: 6  Vision-Model Fallback
section: 6.3 Questions the owner may want to weigh
text:
6.3 Questions the owner may want to weigh
Sending page images to an outside service shares the journal text with that provider. The owner has cleared the material for publication, but should confirm that is acceptable for the chosen provider’s terms.

title: 7  Proofreading
text:
7.1 Using the app
The proofreading step turns OCR drafts into checked text. It is a small Shiny app that shows the page scan beside an editable text box.
From the project root:
A page saved unchanged is recorded as confirmed, so a page checked and found correct counts as done.

title: 7  Proofreading
text:
source("R/proofread.R")
run_proofread()

Left: the page image, either with flagged words boxed in red (half size) or the clean full-resolution crop. A slider zooms.
Right: the text, starting from the OCR draft. A [?word] mark means the OCR was unsure of that word. Retype it without the mark.
Sidebar: filters for tier (tiers A and B by default), volume and status (all, to do, done), plus the page list with Previous and Next.
Saving: Save, or Save and next. Edits are also saved automatically when you change page. A badge above the box shows unsaved changes, and the browser warns before the tab is closed with unsaved edits. A page you only view is not recorded.

title: 7  Proofreading
text:
7.2 The corrections file
Every save writes one row to data/corrections.csv. The file is committed, so the full history of human changes lives in version control.







Column
Meaning




page_id
For example vol1_p016. One row per page; the latest save wins


status
edited (text differs from the OCR draft) or confirmed (checked, unchanged)


corrected_text
The full page text as saved, including any [?word] marks left unresolved


saved_at
Timestamp



The file is written to a temporary name and then renamed, so a crash cannot leave a half-written file.

title: 7  Proofreading
text:
7.3 Merging corrections
apply_corrections() joins the corrections to the page table. A corrected page replaces the OCR draft; every other page keeps it. The result has final_text and a source column (edited, confirmed or ocr_draft), so any page can be traced to where its text came from. Marks left in the text stay visible, so unresolved words are never hidden.
Corrections work at page level. If a page is later re-OCR’d with better settings, its old correction still takes priority.

text:
7.6 Not yet done
A custom dictionary of names and places would reduce false flags. A fix recorded for one word is not yet applied to the same word elsewhere; each page is corrected on its own.

title: 8  Assembly and Downloads
text:
8.1 Planned outputs
Assembly combines the final text for every page into the files readers will use. All of them come from one table, the output of apply_corrections() (see Proofreading).
Each document is built in its own run. The 1966 Europe journal gets its own DOCX, PDF and CSV, separate from the two WWII volumes.

title: 8  Assembly and Downloads
text:
Output
Contents




Per-page CSV
Volume, page, final text, tier, source (edited, confirmed, ocr_draft), mean confidence


DOCX
One file per document with a title page, page markers and readable body style


Searchable PDF
Not decided: the original scans with an invisible text layer, a typeset transcription, or both


Book chapters
One per volume, generated from the same table

title: 8  Assembly and Downloads
text:
8.2 Open decisions

Which searchable PDF to offer. A text layer over the original scans preserves the look of the typescript but is large; a typeset version is small and easy to read.
PDF engine for the book (LaTeX or Typst).
Whether pages still marked as unreviewed OCR drafts should be published, or held back until checked. The source column makes either choice easy to apply.

Download links will be added to the preface and to this chapter once the files exist.
